o: The dominant hemisphere is usually the right in right-handed people
Last's: one hemisphere, "usually the left in right-handed people", is slightly larger and is the dominant hemisphere. (Last's p. 577)
The under surface of the hemisphere is more irregular than the medial surface

Last's says the under surface is more irregular than the flat medial surface.
The orbital surface is slightly concave, the temporal pole boldly convex and the occipital under surface slopes with the tentorium. (Last's p. 577)
The orbital surface of the frontal lobe is slightly convex

Last's says it is slightly concave, from the impression of the anterior cranial fossa.
It is the temporal pole that is boldly convex. (Last's p. 577)
The under surfaces of the two hemispheres are joined by the cerebral peduncles

Last's: "The under surfaces of the two hemispheres are joined by the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain".
The medial surfaces are joined below the falx by the corpus callosum. (Last's p. 577)

questions.s: Regarding the general plan of the CNS (Last's):
o: The medulla becomes the spinal cord where the first cervical nerve roots emerge

Last's: the medulla passes through the foramen magnum and changes its name to spinal cord where the first cervical nerve roots emerge.
So the junction is at the C1 rootlets, below the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 577)
CSF leaves the ventricles through foramina in the roof of the third ventricle

Its only exit is through foramina in the roof of the fourth ventricle, in the medulla.
The third ventricle roof is a closed tela choroidea. (Last's p. 577)
The cerebellum is part of the brainstem

Last's: the midbrain, pons and medulla collectively form the brainstem.
The cerebellum is part of the hindbrain but not the brainstem. (Last's p. 577)
The diencephalon's main parts are the thalamus and hypothalamus

Last's names the thalamus and hypothalamus as the main parts of the diencephalon, whose cavity is the third ventricle.
Each half of the forebrain is commonly called simply the cerebral hemisphere. (Last's p. 577)

questions.s: Concerning the lateral sulcus and insula (Last's):
o: The lateral sulcus begins on the under surface of the brain

Last's: the deep fissure between frontal and temporal lobes on the under surface continues onto the lateral surface.
The part on the lateral surface is strictly the posterior ramus. (Last's p. 578)
The anterior and ascending rami penetrate the middle frontal gyrus

They penetrate the inferior frontal gyrus, dividing it into orbital, triangular and opercular parts.
On the left these form Broca's area. (Last's p. 578)
The opercular part alone forms the opercula over the insula

Last's says the triangular part, with adjacent parietal and temporal cortex, forms the opercula.
The opercula overlie the insula. (Last's p. 578)
The insula is almost completely surrounded by the circular sulcus

The insula has long and short gyri almost completely surrounded by the circular sulcus.
It is buried beneath the opercula. (Last's p. 578)
Is the only long sulcus to pass on to the medial surface

Last's: "It is the only long sulcus to pass over on to the medial surface of the hemisphere."
On the medial surface it is enclosed in the paracentral lobule. (Last's p. 578-9)
Indents the superior border just in front of the midpoint

It indents the superior border just behind the midpoint.
It passes up from just behind the opercula. (Last's p. 578)
Usually runs directly into the lateral sulcus

Last's: the central sulcus does not usually run directly into the lateral sulcus, a useful point when identifying it.
It is a useful identifying point. (Last's p. 578)
Is enclosed on the medial surface by the paracentral lobule

Just behind the midpoint of the superior border the central sulcus turns onto the medial surface, enclosed in the paracentral lobule.
The leg and perineum areas lie here. (Last's p. 579)

questions.s: Concerning the parietal and occipital lobes (Last's):
o: The posterior end of the lateral sulcus is closed by the supramarginal gyrus

The lateral sulcus and superior temporal sulcus project into the inferior parietal lobule; their ends are capped by the supramarginal and angular gyri respectively.
So supramarginal caps the lateral sulcus, angular caps the superior temporal sulcus. (Last's p. 579)
The angular gyrus caps the posterior end of the lateral sulcus

The angular gyrus caps the superior temporal sulcus.
The supramarginal gyrus caps the lateral sulcus. (Last's p. 579)
The occipital demarcation line slopes downwards at 45° to the preoccipital notch

The line runs from the visible part of the parieto-occipital sulcus down at 45° to the inferior border.
The notch is made by a fold of dura over the transverse sinus. (Last's p. 579)
The parietal lobe is divided into lobules by a vertical sulcus

It is divided by a transverse sulcus into superior and inferior parietal lobules.
The inferior lobule receives the ends of the lateral and superior temporal sulci. (Last's p. 578)

questions.s: Concerning the medial surface of the hemisphere (Last's):
o: The cingulate sulcus lies below the cingulate gyrus

The cingulate gyrus lies above the corpus callosum, with the cingulate sulcus above it.
Above the sulcus is the medial frontal gyrus. (Last's p. 579)
The cuneus lies between the parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci

The wedge-shaped medial occipital surface is the cuneus, limited below by the calcarine sulcus.
In front of it, between the parieto-occipital sulcus and paracentral lobule, is the precuneus. (Last's p. 579)
The stem of the Y-shaped sulcal pattern is the anterior part of the calcarine sulcus

The parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci form a Y on its side.
Its limbs are the parieto-occipital sulcus and the posterior calcarine sulcus. (Last's p. 579)
The precuneus lies between the cuneus and the calcarine sulcus

The precuneus lies between the parieto-occipital sulcus and the paracentral lobule.
The lingual gyrus lies below the calcarine sulcus. (Last's p. 579)
The occipitotemporal sulcus lies lateral to the collateral sulcus

Two long parallel sulci run anteroposteriorly: the occipitotemporal laterally and the collateral medially.
Medial to the collateral sulcus is the parahippocampal gyrus. (Last's p. 581)
The parahippocampal gyrus extends back into the occipital lobe

Last's says the parahippocampal gyrus is confined to the temporal lobe, recurved in front as the uncus.
At the back it may appear continuous with the lingual gyrus. (Last's p. 581)
The lingual gyrus is limited at the medial–inferior border by the collateral sulcus

The lingual gyrus lies below the posterior calcarine sulcus.
The collateral sulcus limits it below. (Last's p. 579)
The tentorial surface is really inferomedial

Because the temporo-occipital surface slopes with the tentorium, much of the medial temporal surface is seen from below.
Last's calls the tentorial surface "really inferomedial". (Last's p. 581)

questions.s: Midline structures on the base of the brain (Last's):
o: The tuber cinereum lies in front of the optic chiasma

The tuber cinereum lies behind the chiasma, with the pituitary stalk projecting from it.
Behind it are the mamillary bodies, then the posterior perforated substance. (Last's p. 581)
The anterior perforated substance lies immediately lateral to the chiasma

On the frontal under surface, immediately lateral to the chiasma, is the anterior perforated substance.
The medial and lateral olfactory striae diverge around it. (Last's p. 581)
The posterior perforated substance lies in front of the mamillary bodies

It lies behind the mamillary bodies, deep in the angle between the cerebral peduncles.
The order from front to back is chiasma, tuber cinereum, mamillary bodies, posterior perforated substance. (Last's p. 581)
The optic tracts diverge around the cerebral peduncles under cover of the temporal lobe

From the chiasma the optic tracts pass back around the peduncles, high up under the temporal lobe.
They reach the lateral geniculate bodies. (Last's p. 581)
The corpus striatum is the caudate nucleus and the putamen

Last's: "the corpus striatum is the collective name for the caudate nucleus and the putamen part of the lentiform nucleus."
Many interconnecting fibres give the striated appearance. (Last's p. 581-2)
The globus pallidus provides the main efferent pathway of the corpus striatum

Fibres from the globus pallidus form the main efferent pathway.
The striatum is the input side, the pallidum the output side. (Last's p. 581-2)
The claustrum lies medial to the putamen

The claustrum is a thin saucer-shaped lamina lateral to the putamen.
Last's says its significance is unknown. (Last's p. 582)
The amygdaloid body lies in the floor of the inferior horn

It is connected with the tip of the tail of the caudate in the roof of the inferior horn.
It is functionally part of the limbic system. (Last's p. 582)
The ansa lenticularis passes dorsal to the subthalamic nucleus

The ansa lenticularis passes ventral, and the ansa fascicularis dorsal, to the subthalamic nucleus.
Both carry pallidal fibres to the thalamus. (Last's p. 582)
The ansa fascicularis passes through the internal capsule

Last's: the ansa fascicularis passes through the fibres of the internal capsule.
So does the subthalamic fasciculus. (Last's p. 582)
The striatum receives fibres mainly from the cortex, thalamus and substantia nigra

The striatum is the input side, receiving mainly from the cerebral cortex, thalamus and substantia nigra.
The pallidum sends fibres to the thalamus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra and reticular formation. (Last's p. 582)
The subthalamic fasciculus links the putamen with the subthalamic nucleus

It interconnects the globus pallidus and the subthalamic nucleus.
It also passes through the internal capsule. (Last's p. 582)
The whole convexity of the caudate projects into the lateral ventricle

Last's: "The whole length of its convexity projects into the lateral ventricle."
It curls round the internal capsule like a hand holding flowers. (Last's p. 581)
The caudate tail joins the amygdaloid body

The body curves round the lateral thalamus and bends forward into the long thin tail joining the amygdaloid body.
The tail lies in the roof of the inferior horn. (Last's p. 581)
The putamen is the small medial part of the lentiform nucleus

The putamen is the large lateral part; the globus pallidus the small medial, bluntly conical part.
The lentiform nucleus is completely buried. (Last's p. 581)
The putamen is joined to the caudate head by fibre bundles through the anterior internal capsule

Myelinated and unmyelinated bundles cross the anterior internal capsule, giving it a striated look.
Hence "corpus striatum". (Last's p. 581-2)

questions.s: Concerning the white matter of the hemisphere (Last's):
o: Most commissural fibres are in the corpus callosum

Most commissural fibres gather in the corpus callosum; a few lie in the anterior, posterior and habenular commissures.
Association (arcuate) fibres stay in their own hemisphere. (Last's p. 583)
The habenular commissure contains association fibres

It is listed with the anterior and posterior commissures as carrying commissural fibres.
Association fibres are confined to one hemisphere. (Last's p. 583)
The corona radiata is intersected by fibres of the corpus callosum

Fibres fan up from the capsule as the corona radiata; "Fibres of the corpus callosum intersect it."
The internal capsule lies lateral to the thalamus and caudate head. (Last's p. 583)
The tail of the caudate curls round medial to the internal capsule

The lentiform nucleus and the tail of the caudate both lie lateral to the capsule.
The capsule lies lateral to the thalamus and the caudate head. (Last's p. 583)
It is bent into a lateral concavity by the globus pallidus

In horizontal section the convex medial border of the lentiform nucleus (the globus pallidus) bends it.
Hence anterior limb, genu and posterior limb. (Last's p. 583)
The genu lies at the apex of the globus pallidus

The genu is the bend, at the apex of the globus pallidus.
Its principal constituents are corticonuclear fibres. (Last's p. 583)
Frontopontine fibres occupy the lateral third of the base of the peduncle

Frontopontine fibres from the anterior limb occupy the medial third.
Parieto-, occipito- and temporopontine fibres occupy the lateral third. (Last's p. 583-4)
Corticospinal fibres occupy the posterior third of the posterior limb

They occupy the anterior two-thirds, right behind the genu.
Thalamocortical fibres lie beside and behind them. (Last's p. 583)

questions.s: Concerning fibres in the internal capsule (Last's):
o: The anterior limb probably carries fibres from the frontal eye field to the oculomotor nucleus

Last's says the anterior limb "also probably contains fibres running from the frontal eye field to the oculomotor nucleus".
They serve the accommodation–convergence reflex. (Last's p. 583)
In the cerebral peduncle, perineum fibres lie medially

In the peduncle the head fibres lie medially and the perineum fibres laterally.
In the capsule the order front to back is head, arm, hand, trunk, leg, perineum. (Last's p. 584)
Corticospinal fibres for the hand lie behind those for the arm

The order behind the corticonuclear fibres is arm, hand, trunk, leg, perineum.
So hand lies between arm and trunk. (Last's p. 584)
The sublentiform part contains the optic radiation

The sublentiform part carries the auditory radiation from the medial geniculate body.
The optic radiation is in the retrolentiform part. (Last's p. 584-5)
The retrolentiform part contains parieto-, occipito- and temporopontine fibres

These corticopontine fibres pass through the retrolentiform part to the lateral third of the peduncle.
It also carries the optic radiation. (Last's p. 584)
The auditory radiation ends in the transverse temporal gyrus without reaching the superior temporal gyrus

Last's says the auditory radiation reaches the auditory area in the superior temporal gyrus.
The area extends from the anterior transverse temporal gyrus onto the superior temporal gyrus. (Last's p. 585-6)
Corticopontine fibres number about 20 million

They form the largest group in the capsule.
Corticonuclear, corticospinal, thalamocortical and optic fibres matter more clinically. (Last's p. 585)
Left capsular lesions can interrupt fibres from Broca's area

Fibres from Broca's area are interrupted in lesions of the left internal capsule.
So loss of speech accompanies right hemiplegia. (Last's p. 584)
It begins at the anterior commissure

It commences at the anterior commissure, at the upper end of the lamina terminalis.
It becomes increasingly thicker as it is traced back. (Last's p. 585)
It becomes thinner from front to back

Traced from the anterior commissure it becomes increasingly thicker.
It ends as the thick rounded splenium. (Last's p. 585)
Its fibres form the roof of the body of the lateral ventricle

They pass across the anterior horn and body, forming the roof of each.
In the temporal lobe they form the tapetum. (Last's p. 586)
The tapetum forms the medial wall of the posterior horn

The tapetum forms the lateral wall of the inferior and posterior horns.
The calcar avis is on the medial wall. (Last's p. 586)
MsII lies on the lateral surface of the frontal lobe

MsII (the supplementary motor area) is on part of the medial surface of the frontal lobe.
It is part of areas 6 and 8. (Last's p. 586)
MsI receives its main inputs from the cerebellum and thalamus

Last's: MsI is where movements are initiated, receiving main inputs from the cerebellum and thalamus.
MsII receives many fibres from the basal nuclei. (Last's p. 586)
In MsI the face is represented the right way up

The body is represented upside down, but the face itself the right way up.
Face lowest, then hand, arm, trunk and leg. (Last's p. 586)
In MsI the arm lies below the hand

From below up: face, hand (very large), arm, trunk, leg.
So the arm lies above the hand. (Last's p. 586)
Broca's area lies below and in front of the face area

It is centred on the pars triangularis, below and in front of the face area.
Damage causes motor aphasia, not laryngeal paralysis. (Last's p. 586)
Wernicke's area is confined to the superior temporal gyrus

It occupies the posterior parts of the superior and middle temporal gyri and extends into the lower parietal lobe.
It is needed to understand speech. (Last's p. 586)
The frontal eye field lies in the posterior part of the middle frontal gyrus

Last's places it in the centre of the middle frontal gyrus (parts of areas 6, 8 and 9).
It serves voluntary eye movements and accommodation. (Last's p. 586)
Last's says the cortex is necessary for localising pain

Conscious appreciation of pain may occur at thalamic level, but the cortex is needed to localise it.
SmII appears associated with pain and temperature. (Last's p. 586)
The gustatory area lies in the upper part of the postcentral gyrus

It lies in the inferior postcentral gyrus (frontoparietal operculum), near the tongue area of SmI.
Taste is near the tongue representation. (Last's p. 586)
The auditory association area is area 22

The auditory area (41, 42) is surrounded on the superior temporal gyrus by area 22.
Both receive the auditory radiation. (Last's p. 586)
The visual area lies along the upper lip only of the anterior calcarine sulcus

It lies along the lower lip of the anterior part and both lips of the posterior part.
It extends about 1 cm onto the lateral surface to the lunate sulcus. (Last's p. 586-7)
The visual association areas lack the stria of Gennari

Areas 18 and 19 adjoin the striate cortex and do not have the stria.
The stria bisects the grey matter of area 17. (Last's p. 587)
The retinal bipolar cells correspond to posterior root ganglion cells

Last's: the peripheral nerves of ordinary sensation are represented in the visual pathway by the bipolar cells.
Ganglion cells are homologous with second-order neurons. (Last's p. 587)
There is one ganglion cell for every 8 rods

There is one ganglion cell for each cone and one for 80 rods.
Ganglion cells lie in the inner retina next to the vitreous. (Last's p. 587)
The optic nerve shows no effective regeneration when divided

It is a tract of CNS white matter, so there is no effective regeneration.
It is enclosed in meninges as far as the sclera. (Last's p. 587)
The optic nerve is sheathed in dura as far as the chiasma

At the optic foramen the dura and arachnoid leave it; it passes on sheathed only in pia.
The chiasma is attached to the anterior floor of the third ventricle. (Last's p. 587)

questions.s: Concerning the optic tract and lateral geniculate body (Last's):
o: The optic tract is supplied mainly by the anterior cerebral artery

The optic tract is supplied chiefly by the anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries.
The chiasma and intracranial optic nerve are supplied by the anterior cerebral. (Last's p. 587)
The lateral geniculate body lies below the pulvinar

It is a small rounded elevation below the pulvinar on the posterior thalamus.
It is part of the thalamus. (Last's p. 587)
Ipsilateral temporal fibres synapse in geniculate layers 1, 4 and 6

Temporal (same-side) fibres synapse in layers 2, 3 and 5.
Nasal (opposite-side) fibres synapse in layers 1, 4 and 6. (Last's p. 587)
The smaller branch of the optic tract passes between the two geniculate bodies

The superior brachium passes down medially between the lateral and medial geniculate bodies.
It ends in the superior colliculus and pretectal nuclei. (Last's p. 587)

questions.s: Concerning the superior colliculus and pretectal nucleus (Last's):
o: The superior colliculi are united by the posterior commissure

They are joined at the entrance to the aqueduct, so general light reflexes are usually bilateral.
Tectobulbar and tectospinal tracts carry them. (Last's p. 588)
Pupillary light reflex fibres synapse in the superior colliculus

They do not synapse in the colliculus but pass bilaterally to each pretectal nucleus.
The pretectal nucleus projects to each Edinger–Westphal nucleus. (Last's p. 588)
Hippocampal lesions spare memory for distant events

Last's: hippocampal lesions cause loss of memory for recent events, while distant memory is retained.
The limbic system serves behaviour, mood and memory. (Last's p. 588)
The pretectal nucleus lies under the lower and medial margin of the superior colliculus

It lies in the tegmentum under the upper and lateral margin of the superior colliculus.
A lesion here gives the Argyll Robertson pupil. (Last's p. 588)

questions.s: Last's lists as components of the limbic system:
o: The septal and piriform areas near the lamina terminalis

These are item (1) in Last's list.
Some also include the hypothalamus and anterior thalamus. (Last's p. 589)
The insula

Last's lists the uncus, insula, and cingulate and parahippocampal gyri together.
There is no universal agreement on the membership. (Last's p. 589)
The claustrum

The claustrum is not in Last's limbic list; its significance is unknown.
The amygdaloid body is listed. (Last's p. 582, 589)
The mamillary body

Last's lists the hippocampus, fimbria, fornix and mamillary body.
Together these form the Papez-type circuit. (Last's p. 589)
There are three groups of neurons from receptor to cortex

Last's: there are two groups of neurons, and the second reaches the cortex without thalamic relay.
Last's calls this unique. (Last's p. 589)
Mitral cell axons pass through the anterior perforated substance

The axons run back in the tract to the anterior perforated substance, through which some reach the uncus.
Others connect with the limbic system. (Last's p. 589)
The olfactory tract is an extension of the white matter of the brain

Last's compares it with the optic nerve.
It lies in the olfactory sulcus beside the gyrus rectus. (Last's p. 589)
The olfactory bulb has no connexions with the hypothalamus

Further synapses connect the bulb with the hypothalamus and brainstem for visceral and somatic effects.
This parallels other sensory pathways. (Last's p. 589)
The anterior parahippocampal gyrus beneath it is the subiculum

Just above the anterior parahippocampal gyrus (the subiculum) lies the hippocampal sulcus, projected into the inferior horn as the hippocampus.
The pes hippocampi looks like clenched knuckles. (Last's p. 588-9)
The alveus is a film of grey matter on the ventricular surface

The alveus is a thin film of white matter.
Its fibres thicken medially into the fimbria. (Last's p. 589)
The dentate gyrus lies between the fimbria and the parahippocampal gyrus

Seen from the medial side, the dentate gyrus lies between them.
It is a small part of the hippocampus. (Last's p. 589)
The fimbria continues as the anterior column of the fornix

The fimbria breaks free as the crus (posterior pillar) of the fornix.
The crura join as the body; the anterior columns arch down in front. (Last's p. 589)
The commissure of the fornix is really a chiasma

Last's: "It is really a chiasma, and is an association tract rather than a true commissure."
It is a partial decussation. (Last's p. 589)
Its columns pass only behind the anterior commissure

The columns pass both in front of and behind the anterior commissure.
Anterior fibres go to the septal nuclei; posterior fibres to the thalamus and mamillary body. (Last's p. 589)
Its anterior fibres end in the septum pellucidum
They pass mainly to the septal nuclei near the lamina terminalis, "not in the septum pellucidum". (Last's p. 589)
Its anterior columns form the anterior margins of the interventricular foramina

The conjoined columns arch down in front of the anterior poles of the thalami.
The foramen lies between column and thalamus. (Last's p. 589)

questions.s: Concerning the ventricles and choroid plexuses (Last's):
o: The lateral ventricle plexuses secrete the bulk of the CSF

Last's: this pair is large and highly vascular and secretes the bulk of the CSF.
The fourth ventricle plexus makes only a small contribution. (Last's p. 590)
The fourth ventricle plexus is continuous with that of the third

The fourth ventricle plexus is separate.
Lateral and third ventricle plexuses are continuous through the interventricular foramen. (Last's p. 590)
The central canal extends into the upper end of the filum terminale

Below the fourth ventricle the central canal runs through the cord into the upper filum.
The only apertures are in the fourth ventricle roof. (Last's p. 590)
Asymmetry of the lateral ventricles is commonest anteriorly

Asymmetry, especially posteriorly, is the rule.
The midline cavities are symmetrical. (Last's p. 590)
The choroid fissure should be regarded as the medial wall of the body and inferior horn

Last's says so explicitly.
The plexus is invaginated through it. (Last's p. 590)
The parahippocampal sulcus shows as a convexity in the ventricle

The parahippocampal, calcarine and collateral sulci all indent the cavity.
Elsewhere the walls are white matter. (Last's p. 590)
The interventricular foramen lies in front of the anterior column of the fornix

It lies behind the anterior column, between it and the anterior pole of the thalamus.
It leads into the third ventricle. (Last's p. 590)
The choroid plexus of the body extends into the anterior horn

It does not; it passes through the interventricular foramen into the third ventricle.
There is none in the anterior or posterior horns. (Last's p. 590)

questions.s: The body and horns of the lateral ventricle (Last's):
o: The thalamostriate vein lies in the groove between thalamus and caudate

The floor of the body is thalamus and caudate body, with the thalamostriate groove between.
The vein is the more important content. (Last's p. 590)
The fornix is a roof structure that appears to lie on the floor

Last's: the fornix "is actually a roof structure — a roof can collapse upon a floor".
The plexus projects between fornix and thalamus. (Last's p. 590)
The posterior horn is the most constant horn

Last's: the posterior horn is the most variably developed and may be absent.
A large calcar avis can obliterate it. (Last's p. 591)
The bulb of the posterior horn is formed by the forceps major

The upper medial convexity is the bulb (forceps major); the lower is the calcar avis.
The floor convexity is the collateral eminence. (Last's p. 591)
It is the largest horn

Last's: "The inferior horn is the largest."
Its floor is the hippocampus medially and collateral eminence laterally. (Last's p. 591)
The fimbria forms the upper lip of the choroid fissure in the inferior horn

The fimbria forms the lower lip; the fornix forms the upper lip in the body.
They are continuous around the convexity of the C. (Last's p. 591)
The amygdaloid body lies medial to the anterior perforated substance

It lies to the lateral side of the anterior perforated substance.
It makes a convexity in the roof at the tip of the horn. (Last's p. 591)
The inferior horn is closed laterally by the tapetum

Last's: "The inferior horn is closed laterally by the white matter of the tapetum."
The collateral trigone is where posterior and inferior horns diverge. (Last's p. 592)

questions.s: Because the lateral ventricle is C-shaped (Last's):
o: Structures around the convexity lie in the roof of the body and the floor of the inferior horn

Convexity structures (fornix–fimbria) are in the body roof and inferior horn floor.
Concavity structures are in the body floor and inferior horn roof. (Last's p. 592)
The caudate tail lies in the floor of the inferior horn

The caudate lies in the concavity, so its tail is in the roof of the inferior horn.
Its head and body are in the floor of the anterior horn and body. (Last's p. 591-2)
Any section must cut C-shaped structures in two places

Last's notes this implication for vertical or horizontal sections.
The internal capsule lies in the concavity of the caudate. (Last's p. 592)
The internal capsule lies in the convexity of the caudate

The internal capsule is contained within the concavity of the caudate nucleus.
The caudate lies within the concavity of the ventricle. (Last's p. 592)
The lamina terminalis extends from the rostrum to the top of the optic chiasma

It runs between the hemispheres from the rostrum of the corpus callosum to the top of the chiasma.
It contains the anterior commissure above. (Last's p. 592)
The anterior commissure joins the two piriform areas

Last's: it "joins the two piriform areas of the cortex" and is a commissure of the archaeopallium.
It lies behind the upper end of the lamina terminalis. (Last's p. 593-4)
The cavity of the septum pellucidum is lined with ependyma

It is lined with pia mater, not ependyma, and has no connexion with the ventricles.
So "fifth ventricle" should be avoided. (Last's p. 593)
The interthalamic adhesion carries fibres between the thalami

Last's: it is not a commissure and there is no interchange of fibres.
It is present in 60% of brains. (Last's p. 593-4)
The median eminence has no blood–brain barrier

Last's calls the median eminence one of the few regions with no blood–brain barrier.
It lies at the base of the infundibulum. (Last's p. 594)
The mamillary bodies mark the inside of the third ventricle

Last's: the dependent mamillary bodies and posterior perforated substance make no mark inside the ventricle.
The chiasma does indent it. (Last's p. 594)
The infundibulum is hollow and the pituitary stalk solid

Behind the chiasma the hollow infundibulum projects down to become the solid stalk.
The infundibular recess is its hollow. (Last's p. 594)
The subthalamic nucleus lies on the lateral side of the internal capsule

It is a small lens-shaped body on the medial side of the capsule, beside the substantia nigra.
It belongs functionally to the basal nuclei. (Last's p. 594)

questions.s: The roof of the third ventricle (Last's):
o: The interventricular foramen is roofed by bare pia mater

Pia sweeps from the under surface of the fornix body to the anterior pole of the thalamus.
This is the anterior limit of the tela choroidea. (Last's p. 594)
The medullary striae join posteriorly in the posterior commissure

They join in a U-shaped loop, the habenular commissure.
Last's says it is probably olfactory, like the anterior commissure. (Last's p. 594)
The pial roof bulges back as the suprapineal recess

The roof is variably slack posteriorly and bulges back as the suprapineal recess.
It is lined with ependyma. (Last's p. 594)
The hypothalamic groove curves down above the thalamus

It curves down from the interventricular foramen below the thalamus towards the aqueduct.
Below it is the hypothalamus. (Last's p. 594)
The pretectal nuclei lie just cranial to the superior colliculi

They lie at the junction of midbrain and diencephalon, just cranial to the superior colliculi.
They serve the pupillary light reflex, not general light reflexes. (Last's p. 607)
The Edinger–Westphal nucleus lies in the caudal part of the oculomotor nucleus

It lies near the midline in the cranial part of the nucleus.
Its fibres relay in the ciliary ganglion. (Last's p. 607)
The oculomotor nerve emerges on the medial side of the base of the peduncle

It passes ventrally through the red nucleus to emerge medially from the base of the peduncle.
The nucleus lies ventral to the aqueduct. (Last's p. 607)
The trochlear nucleus lies dorsal to the aqueduct

It lies ventral to the aqueduct at inferior colliculus level; only the nerves decussate dorsal to it.
It emerges through the superior medullary velum behind the inferior colliculus. (Last's p. 607)
It lies just ventral to the oculomotor nucleus

The red nucleus lies in the tegmentum just ventral to the third nerve nucleus, whose axons pass through it.
It is slightly larger than a full-sized pea. (Last's p. 607)
Its efferent fibres decussate at the level of the superior colliculi

Its efferents decussate at inferior colliculus level, in the ventral tegmental decussation.
They descend to the pontine nuclei and cord. (Last's p. 607, 612)
Last's says it is not associated with any known disease

Despite its size it seems of little functional significance in man.
It receives from the opposite dentate nucleus. (Last's p. 607)
It receives fibres from the ipsilateral dentate nucleus

It receives from the dentate nucleus of the opposite cerebellar hemisphere via the superior peduncle.
It also connects with cortex and globus pallidus. (Last's p. 607)
The mesencephalic nucleus lies medial to the aqueduct

It lies in the central grey matter lateral to the aqueduct, throughout the length of the midbrain.
It is long and slender. (Last's p. 607)
The mesencephalic nucleus receives proprioceptive fibres from the orbital and facial muscles

It receives from the muscles of mastication, orbit and face, and perhaps the tongue.
It is unique as first-neuron cells inside the CNS. (Last's p. 607)
The midbrain is supplied by the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

They supply it as they curl round the cerebral peduncle.
Central branches enter the crura to the substantia nigra and red nucleus. (Last's p. 607-8)
Midbrain veins drain mainly into the great cerebral vein

They drain mostly into the basal vein; some blood from the colliculi enters the great cerebral vein.
The basal vein passes round the peduncle. (Last's p. 608)
The trigeminal is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the pons

Its point of emergence marks the change of name from pons to middle cerebellar peduncle.
It has a large sensory and small motor root. (Last's p. 608)
The basilar artery always lies in the midline groove of the pons

It may or may not lie in the groove; usually it curves gently to one side.
It lies in the pontine cistern. (Last's p. 608)
The lingula of the cerebellum lies on the superior medullary velum

The pontine roof of the fourth ventricle is the superior medullary velum, with the lingula on it.
It is attached to the superior cerebellar peduncles. (Last's p. 608)
The upper pons contains the widest part of the floor of the fourth ventricle

The lower pons contains the widest part of the floor.
Upper pons sections show a closed, almost rectangular ventricle. (Last's p. 608)

questions.s: Concerning the pontine nuclei of cranial nerves (Last's):
o: The trigeminal motor nucleus lies in the lower pons

It is in the upper pons below the lateral part of the floor of the fourth ventricle.
Its fibres emerge at the junction of pons and middle cerebellar peduncle. (Last's p. 609)
The main sensory nucleus of V lies lateral to the motor nucleus

The main sensory nucleus lies lateral to the motor nucleus and receives touch fibres.
Pain and temperature go to the spinal nucleus. (Last's p. 609)
The facial nucleus is not responsible for the facial colliculus

The colliculus is the abducent nucleus plus overlying facial fibres.
The facial nucleus lies deeper and further from the midline. (Last's p. 609)
The inferior salivary nucleus lies above the superior salivary nucleus

The superior salivary nucleus lies alongside the facial nucleus; the inferior is lower, just above the pontomedullary junction.
The inferior sends fibres with IX to the otic ganglion. (Last's p. 609)

questions.s: Concerning the vestibulocochlear nuclei and pons (Last's):
o: Vestibular fibres pass anterior to the inferior cerebellar peduncle

They emerge from the internal acoustic meatus and pass anterior to the inferior peduncle to the vestibular nuclei.
Many vestibular fibres then pass back into that peduncle. (Last's p. 609)
The cochlear nuclei are mainly pontine

The cochlear nuclei are mainly medullary but extend into the lower pons.
Vestibular and cochlear nuclei are separate. (Last's p. 609)
Pontine veins drain into the inferior petrosal sinuses and basilar plexus

Venous return from the pons is into the inferior petrosal sinuses and the basilar plexus.
The pons is supplied mainly by pontine branches of the basilar. (Last's p. 609)
The pontine reticular formation lies ventral to the pontine nuclei

It lies dorsal to the pontine nuclei and their intermingled fibres.
It continues down into the medulla and upper cord. (Last's p. 609)

questions.s: Concerning the surface of the medulla (Last's):
o: It lies almost vertically from a line joining the jugular tubercles to the atlas

Last's describes this course, passing through the foramen magnum.
It lies in the vallecula between the cerebellar hemispheres. (Last's p. 609)
The sixth nerve emerges between the pons and the olive

VI emerges between the pons and the pyramid.
The main part of VII emerges between the pons and the olive. (Last's p. 609)
VIII emerges at the junction of the pons and the inferior cerebellar peduncle

The nervus intermedius and VIII emerge at the junction of pons and inferior peduncle.
IX, X and cranial XI emerge lateral to the olive. (Last's p. 609)
XII emerges as a single bundle lateral to the olive

XII emerges by two small groups of rootlets between the pyramid and olive.
The rootlets lateral to the olive are IX, X and XI. (Last's p. 609)
The inferior cerebellar peduncle enters the cerebellum medial to and below the flocculus
Lateral to the olive the lateral surface is the inferior peduncle, entering the cerebellum medial to and below the flocculus. (Last's p. 609)
The sensory decussation lies below the motor decussation

Visible pyramidal decussation characterizes the lowest medulla; the lemniscal decussation is slightly higher.
So the sensory decussation lies above the motor. (Last's p. 610)
The trigeminal tubercle is usually less well defined than the gracile and cuneate tubercles
The closed medulla shows gracile and cuneate tubercles and the usually less well-defined trigeminal tubercle. (Last's p. 610)
The vagal trigone lies medial to the hypoglossal trigone

The hypoglossal trigone is adjacent to the midline with the vagal trigone lateral to it.
Higher up laterally are the vestibular area and medullary striae. (Last's p. 610)

questions.s: The nucleus of the tractus solitarius (Last's):
o: Its cells are the most tightly packed of any brainstem nucleus

Last's says so.
The two nuclei meet in the lowest open medulla, forming a V. (Last's p. 610)
Its lower part receives the taste fibres

Its upper part receives taste fibres (chorda tympani, lingual branch of IX, internal laryngeal).
The rest receives visceral afferents of IX and X. (Last's p. 610)
Some of its cells form the inspiratory centre

Last's: "Some of its cells form the inspiratory centre."
It serves cough, sneeze, gag and vomiting reflexes. (Last's p. 610)
It receives taste fibres from the external laryngeal nerve

The internal laryngeal branch carries the taste fibres (epiglottic region).
The external laryngeal is motor to cricothyroid. (Last's p. 610)
The upper part of the nucleus ambiguus supplies the larynx

The upper part supplies the palate, middle part pharynx and oesophagus, lowest part the larynx.
Stylopharyngeus is supplied via IX. (Last's p. 611)
The inferior olivary nucleus opens towards the opposite inferior cerebellar peduncle

It is a crenated C-shaped sac, open towards the opposite peduncle.
Olivocerebellar fibres decussate to enter it. (Last's p. 611)
The accessory cuneate nucleus carries upper limb proprioception to the cerebellum

Its cuneocerebellar fibres pass via the inferior peduncle.
This replaces the spinocerebellar route for the upper limb. (Last's p. 611)
The spinal nucleus of V lies medial to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

It lies lateral to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
It continues down from the pons. (Last's p. 611)

questions.s: Concerning the reticular formation and area postrema (Last's):
o: The vital centres are not anatomically demonstrable as distinct nuclei

Last's: they are not distinct nuclei, but disturbing this area results in death.
Last's keeps the term "vital centres". (Last's p. 611)
The area postrema lies lateral to each gracile nucleus

It lies on the medial side of each gracile nucleus at the lower angle of the ventricle.
It is the vomiting centre and chemoreceptor trigger zone. (Last's p. 611)
The reticular formation is responsible for the wakeful component of consciousness

Last's credits it with the "alert" or "wakeful" component.
It also influences motor, sensory, autonomic and endocrine activity. (Last's p. 611)
The reticular formation receives from the ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere

It receives from the opposite cerebellar hemisphere via the dentate nucleus.
It receives from the same-side cortex via striatum and pallidum. (Last's p. 611)
There is loss of pain and temperature on the same side of the face

The uncrossed spinal tract of V is damaged.
The crossed spinal lemniscus gives opposite-side body loss. (Last's p. 612)
There is hemiplegia on the opposite side

Hemiplegia is a feature of the medial medullary syndrome (pyramid).
The lateral syndrome spares the pyramid. (Last's p. 612)
Loss of nucleus ambiguus function gives dysphonia and dysphagia

The vocal fold, palatal and pharyngeal muscles on that side are paralysed.
Vestibular involvement gives vertigo and nystagmus. (Last's p. 612)
There is an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome

The descending sympathetic pathway is interrupted.
It is the "syndrome of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery". (Last's p. 612)
Corticonuclear fibres collect in the lateral part of the crus

They collect in the most medial part of the central three-fifths of the crus.
Some go straight to III and IV nuclei. (Last's p. 612)
The lower part of the facial nucleus is supplied only by the opposite cortex

Last's names it the most important exception to bilateral innervation.
Most motor cranial nuclei are bilaterally innervated. (Last's p. 612)
In the crus the leg fibres lie medial to the arm fibres

Arm fibres lie medial to leg fibres in the central three-fifths of the crus.
Head fibres are most medial. (Last's p. 612)
Uncrossed anterior corticospinal fibres also eventually cross in the cord

The few uncrossed fibres form the anterior corticospinal tract but also eventually cross.
All end in the anterior horn. (Last's p. 612)
Frontopontine fibres occupy the medial one-fifth of the crus

On p. 612 Last's gives the medial one-fifth (p. 583 says medial third).
Temporo-, parieto- and occipitopontine fibres occupy the lateral one-fifth. (Last's p. 612)
Corticopontine fibres arise only from the frontal lobe

They arise from many areas of all four lobes and pass through all parts of the capsule.
Pontine axons then decussate into the middle peduncle. (Last's p. 612)
The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the tectospinal tracts
Just dorsal to the ventral (rubrospinal) decussation is the smaller dorsal tegmental decussation of the tectospinal tracts. (Last's p. 612)
The rubrospinal tracts decussate after descending into the pons
They decussate immediately, in the ventral tegmental decussation, before passing down. (Last's p. 612)
The medial longitudinal bundle extends from the upper border of the midbrain to the upper cervical cord

It lies just ventral to the periaqueductal grey and stays near the midline.
It links vestibular nuclei with III, IV and VI. (Last's p. 613)
The tectospinal and rubrospinal tracts descend to the lumbar cord

Last's: they descend no farther than the cervical region.
They assist head and neck movements. (Last's p. 613)
The lateral reticulospinal tract arises from the medullary reticular formation

Lateral from medullary, anterior from pontine reticular formation.
They mix with corticospinal fibres in the cord. (Last's p. 613)
The descending sympathetic tract runs with the medial lemniscus

Its fibres run in the region of the spinal lemniscus.
They end in the thoracolumbar lateral horn. (Last's p. 613)
The medial lemniscus deviates laterally as it ascends through the pons and midbrain

It starts near the midline, then deviates laterally before reaching the thalamus.
It is joined by the trigeminal lemniscus. (Last's p. 613)
The spinal lemniscus enlarges as it ascends

It quickly becomes much smaller, as most fibres end in the reticular formation.
It runs at the lateral then dorsal edge of the medial lemniscus. (Last's p. 613)
The trapezoid body and lateral lemniscus contain cell stations

They connect with the extraocular nuclei via the medial longitudinal bundle.
The lateral lemniscus ends in the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate body. (Last's p. 613)
The anterior spinocerebellar tract enters the inferior cerebellar peduncle

The posterior tract enters the inferior peduncle; the anterior continues up to the superior peduncle.
Both lie at the lateral margin of the lower medulla. (Last's p. 613)

questions.s: Concerning the roof of the fourth ventricle (Last's):
o: The inferior medullary velum arises from the base of the flocculus

The upper medullary roof is covered by the inferior medullary velum from the base of the flocculus.
The lowest part is ependyma and pia only. (Last's p. 613)
The median aperture opens into the pontine cistern

The median aperture opens into the cerebellomedullary cistern.
The lateral apertures open into the pontine cistern, just behind VIII. (Last's p. 613)
The lower margin of the roof is attached to the gracile and cuneate tubercles

It is perforated by the midline median aperture (of Magendie).
CSF escapes into the cerebellomedullary cistern. (Last's p. 613)
The lateral aperture opens posteriorly into the cerebellomedullary cistern

It opens anteriorly, just behind VIII, into the pontine cistern.
The lateral recess runs round behind the inferior peduncle. (Last's p. 613)

questions.s: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle (Last's):
o: Begins at the lateral aperture by a branch of PICA

It commences at the lateral aperture, just below the flocculus.
It turns medially to meet its fellow. (Last's p. 614)
Forms an H-shaped plexus

The two L-shaped halves form a T-shaped plexus with a double central stem.
It indents the medullary part of the roof. (Last's p. 614)
Drains into the straight sinus
Its veins drain back into the occipital sinus. (Last's p. 614)
Makes only a small contribution to the total CSF

It is separate from the third and lateral ventricle plexuses.
The lateral plexuses secrete the bulk. (Last's p. 590, 614)

questions.s: The floor of the fourth ventricle (Last's):
o: The medullary striae are aberrant fibres from the pontine nuclei

They cross the widest part of the floor, destined for the cerebellum.
They lie between pontine and medullary parts. (Last's p. 614)
The locus caeruleus lies in the inferior fovea

It lies in the upper part of the superior fovea; its pigmented cells are noradrenergic.
It is part of the reticular formation. (Last's p. 614)
The medullary part of the floor is smaller than the pontine part

Last's says so.
The inferior fovea divides it into hypoglossal and vagal trigones. (Last's p. 614)
The hypoglossal trigone has its apex pointing upwards
The medial (hypoglossal) trigone has its apex down; the lateral (vagal) apex upwards. (Last's p. 614)
Some CSF drains through the cribriform plate into nasal tissues

There is some drainage through the cribriform plate into the nose and so to cervical lymphatics.
Most resorption is through arachnoid granulations. (Last's p. 614)
Changes in arterial pressure are quickly reflected in CSF pressure
Arterial pressure changes have little effect; raised venous pressure is quickly reflected. (Last's p. 614)
There is a brain/CSF barrier

Last's: there is no brain/CSF barrier, but there is a blood/CSF barrier.
It is due to ependymal tight junctions over the choroid plexus. (Last's p. 614)
The subarachnoid space holds about 75 ml in the spinal part

Of 100 ml subarachnoid CSF, about 75 ml is spinal and 25 ml cranial.
The ventricles hold about 30 ml. (Last's p. 614)
The sensory nuclei of cranial nerves are second-neuron cell bodies

First neurons lie in ganglia on the nerves.
The mesencephalic nucleus is the solitary exception. (Last's p. 615)
The trigeminal motor nucleus supplies tensor tympani in Last's list
Last's lists mastication muscles, mylohyoid and tensor palati. (Last's p. 615)
Last's lists four vestibular and two cochlear nuclei
Six special sensory nuclei: two cochlear in the inferior cerebellar peduncle, four vestibular. (Last's p. 615)
The spinal accessory arises from the upper three cervical segments
Last's: anterior horn cells of the upper five or six cervical segments. (Last's p. 616)
Facial taste fibres from the soft palate travel in the greater petrosal nerve
The nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives chorda tympani taste from the tongue and greater petrosal taste from the soft palate. (Last's p. 615)
Facial somatic fibres from the external meatus go to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

They go to the trigeminal sensory nuclei.
So do general sensory fibres of IX. (Last's p. 615)
IX carries ordinary sensation from the tonsil to the trigeminal nuclei

Somatic sensation from tongue, palate, pharynx and tonsil goes to the trigeminal sensory nuclei.
Taste and baroreceptor fibres go to the tractus solitarius. (Last's p. 615)
The vagus carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue

The vagus carries taste only from the epiglottis.
The posterior third is IX. (Last's p. 615-16)
Absent corneal reflexes test pontine trigeminal–facial connexions

Last's: corneal reflexes test pontine connexions between V and VII.
Pressure on the supraorbital margin tests the same. (Last's p. 616)
The apnoea test requires PaCO2 above 30 mm Hg
It requires PaCO2 above 50 mm Hg (6.7 kPa). (Last's p. 616)
Absent response to a tracheal catheter tests vagal medullary connexions
Gag and bronchial stimulation responses test vagal connexions. (Last's p. 616)
Hypothermia excludes the diagnosis permanently
Drugs, hypothermia and endocrine or metabolic disturbance must be excluded first, since they produce functional damage. (Last's p. 616)
The horizontal fissure separates palaeocerebellum from neocerebellum

The horizontal fissure is the deepest but of no functional significance.
The primary fissure separates palaeo- from neocerebellum. (Last's p. 617)
The highest part of the cerebellum lies at the tentorial notch
The superior surface slopes concavely up to the highest part at the notch. (Last's p. 616)
The nodule lies highest of the three inferior vermian lobules
The inferior vermis has pyramid, uvula and nodule; the nodule lies highest, on the fourth ventricle roof. (Last's p. 617)
The paraflocculus is attached mainly to the uvula

It is attached mainly to the pyramid and lies beneath the flocculus.
It is enormous in marine mammals. (Last's p. 617)
Archaeocerebellar lesions cause trunk ataxia without nystagmus

Last's: "there is no nystagmus, no tremor and no alteration of muscle reflexes."
Fine movements are well performed. (Last's p. 618)
Palaeocerebellar lesions reduce muscle reflexes
They cause great disturbance of posture with increased reflexes. (Last's p. 618)
Neocerebellar lesions cause pendular jerks and dysdiadochokinesia
Hypotonia, diminished or pendulum jerks, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia. (Last's p. 618)
Cerebellar intention tremor is worst at rest
It is absent at rest and best seen towards the end of the finger–nose test. (Last's p. 618)
The dentate nucleus is open towards the superior peduncle

It is a large crenated crescent like the inferior olive, open towards the superior peduncle.
Its efferents go to the opposite red nucleus and thalamus. (Last's p. 618)
The globose nucleus belongs to the archaeocerebellum

The fastigial nucleus is archaeocerebellar; emboliform and globose are palaeocerebellar.
EGF from lateral to medial. (Last's p. 618)
Purkinje dendrites lie at right angles to the long axis of a folium

All branches lie in one plane, like a tree on a wall.
Adjacent dendrites line up like telegraph poles. (Last's p. 618)
Mossy fibres activate Purkinje cells directly
Climbing fibres do; mossy fibres act through granular and basket cells. (Last's p. 618)
A climbing fibre directly activates one Purkinje cell

A mossy fibre indirectly activates many hundred Purkinje cells.
Climbing fibres weave around Purkinje dendrites in the molecular layer. (Last's p. 618-19)
Most granule cell axons end on basket cells

Some arborize around the few basket cells; the majority end directly on Purkinje dendrites.
Granule axons bifurcate in a T. (Last's p. 619)
Some vestibulocerebellar fibres enter the fastigial nucleus without reaching the cortex

Last's lists this among clinically unimportant exceptions to the rule that afferents go to cortex.
A few cerebellovestibular fibres leave directly from cortex. (Last's p. 619)
Efferent cerebellar fibres arise mainly from the cortex

As a general rule efferents arise from subcortical nuclei, not the cortex.
Afferents pass directly to the cortex. (Last's p. 619)
The superior peduncle carries tectocerebellar fibres
It contains dentate efferents, the anterior spinocerebellar tract and tectocerebellar fibres. (Last's p. 619)
The cerebellovestibular tract goes to the opposite vestibular nucleus
It runs from the roof nuclei to the vestibular nucleus of the same side, in the inferior peduncle. (Last's p. 619)
Cuneocerebellar fibres are posterior external arcuate fibres
They arise from the accessory cuneate nucleus and enter the inferior peduncle for the anterior lobe. (Last's p. 619)
Olivocerebellar fibres go mainly to the anterior lobe
They go to the posterior lobe (neocerebellum) from the opposite olive. (Last's p. 619)
PICA is the largest branch of the vertebral artery

It is one of the most tortuous arteries in the body.
It arises near the lower end of the olive. (Last's p. 619)
PICA passes above the hypoglossal rootlets
It spirals round the medulla below the hypoglossal rootlets, then between IX and X rootlets. (Last's p. 619)
AICA arises from the lower part of the basilar and supplies the flocculus
It runs on the inferior surface and may give the labyrinthine artery. (Last's p. 619)
The superior cerebellar artery winds round the peduncle above the fourth nerve

It winds round the cerebral peduncle below IV.
It supplies the superior surface. (Last's p. 619)
In the fetus the cord reaches S2

It reaches the lower limit of the dura at S2 vertebra.
At birth the conus is at L3. (Last's p. 620)
The conus reaches its permanent level by about 5 years
It reaches L1 or L2 at about 20 years. (Last's p. 620)
The posterior median septum of the cord attaches to an arachnoid septum
It is attached to the incomplete posterior median septum of arachnoid. (Last's p. 619)
The lumbosacral enlargement lies opposite vertebrae L2 to S3

Segments L2–S3 lie opposite vertebrae T9–L1.
The cervical enlargement (C5–T1) lies opposite C3–T1. (Last's p. 620)
No spinal nerve lies strictly within the vertebral canal
Roots unite in the intervertebral foramina, outside the theca. (Last's p. 620)
The posterior root ganglia of cervical nerves lie within the foramina
Cervical ganglia lie just lateral to the foramina, in contact with the vertebral artery. (Last's p. 620)
From C1 to L1 anterior roots pass in front of the denticulate ligament

Anterior roots pass in front, posterior roots behind.
They evaginate the dura between denticulations. (Last's p. 620)
Each posterior root is formed by three or four rootlets
Anterior roots have three or four; posterior roots have several, attached vertically. (Last's p. 620)

questions.s: Internal structure of the spinal cord (Last's):
o: The central canal extends into the upper few millimetres of the filum terminale
It is lined by ependyma. (Last's p. 621)
The anterior horn reaches the surface of the cord
The posterior horn stretches to the surface; the anterior falls short. (Last's p. 621)
Ventral cells of the lateral anterior horn supply proximal limb muscles
Medial cells supply the trunk, lateral cells the limbs; ventral lateral cells proximal, dorsal lateral cells distal. (Last's p. 621)
The posterior white columns are largest in the lumbar region

They are largest in the cervical region.
Anterior horns are largest in cervical and lumbar regions. (Last's p. 621)
Lamina V is a main source of anterolateral tract fibres
Laminae III–VI form the nucleus proprius; lamina V is a main source of spinothalamic and spinoreticular fibres. (Last's p. 622)
The thoracic nucleus lies in lamina IX

It lies in the medial part of lamina VII.
Lamina IX holds alpha and gamma motor neurons. (Last's p. 622)
Sacral parasympathetic cells lie in the same position as thoracic sympathetic cells

Last's notes they are in exactly the same position in the cord.
Both form a small lateral horn. (Last's p. 622)
Rexed's laminae were first defined in the human cord
The original research was on the cat, confirmed for primates. (Last's p. 622)
First-neuron cell bodies always lie outside the CNS, except the trigeminal proprioceptive ones

The mesencephalic nucleus is the one odd exception.
Second neurons are in cord or brainstem, third in thalamus. (Last's p. 622)
The posterior white column contains descending as well as ascending fibres
It is wholly occupied by ascending gracile and cuneate fibres. (Last's p. 622)
Except in the posterior columns, cord tracts have no sharp boundaries
There is much intermingling of fibres. (Last's p. 622)
The anterolateral tract is confined to the lateral white column

It extends into the anterior white column.
It carries pain and temperature. (Last's p. 622)
